solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Corporation installing computers in a reflective metal (8)

indicators.note: to install something is to fit it inside, so the tummy takes the other letters in
a reflection shows things back to front, so the letters of 'in a' are turned round

blocks.note: a corporation is an old jokey word for a paunch, a tum
information technology
IN A, reflected to read ANI

annotation.surface: A company fitting out its computers inside a shiny metal casing.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Corporation’ reads as a business, but it is the old slang for a large belly. The tum opens after its T to take IT and the mirrored IN A.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain definition: titanium is a strong, light, silvery metallic element.

clue.text: Dependency on me fails to work (4,2,3)

indicators.note: letters set to work are put into action and rearranged into something useful

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: Someone lamenting that another's reliance on them isn't working out.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Dependency’ looks like emotional reliance, the start of a personal complaint, but it is the political sense: the Isle of Man is a Crown dependency, a self-governing island in the Irish Sea under the British Crown.
annotation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man is not part of the UK but a Crown dependency, so it is literally a dependency.

clue.text: Nemesis of Rachel almost destroyed (4-3)

indicators.note: almost the whole word, so the last letter is dropped
something destroyed is broken up, so its letters are scattered and reassembled

blocks.note: used as is
RACHEL without its last letter

annotation.surface: Someone whose worst enemy was Rachel, who has nearly been wiped out.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Of’ looks like a joining word between definition and wordplay, but its letters are part of the anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: A nemesis is a person's principal enemy, their arch-foe.

clue.text: American’s reaction to smart Scotsman’s clothing (5)

indicators.note: clothing wraps round a body, so the Scotsman's name goes round the cry

blocks.note: Ian is a typically Scottish first name
what you say when something smarts, or stings

annotation.surface: An American commenting on a well-dressed Scotsman's outfit.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Smart’ reads as well dressed, which fits the clothing picture, but it is the verb: a sting that makes you say OW. The first ’s stands for ‘is’.
annotation.definitionFit: An Iowan comes from Iowa, a state in the Midwest, so is an American.

clue.text: What you should call surgeon hiding a blemish (3)

indicators.note: to hide something is to keep it inside, so the title holds the A

blocks.note: in Britain surgeons are addressed as Mr, not Dr
used as is

annotation.surface: Advice on how to address a surgeon who is covering up a scar.
annotation.walkthrough: A British custom: a surgeon, once qualified, drops ‘Doctor’ and goes back to Mr, Ms or Mrs. Here the verb sense of ‘blemish’ is meant: to mar is to spoil.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: to spoil the look of something.

clue.text: Shop U-turning about craftsman (6)

indicators.note: a U-turn sends you back the way you came, so the letters of 'about' run backwards

blocks.note: the Co-op, a British chain of shops
RE means about; turned round it reads ER

annotation.surface: A shop doing an about-turn on the craftsman it employs.
annotation.walkthrough: The Co-op is a long-established British cooperative that runs grocery stores.
annotation.definitionFit: A cooper is a craftsman who makes and repairs barrels and casks.

clue.text: Real ale fans drinking last of Singapore sling and avoiding shots? (6-3)

indicators.note: what you drink goes inside you, so the campaigners take in the letter
take the final letter of the word that follows

blocks.note: CAMRA is the Campaign for Real Ale, a British consumer group for traditional beer
the final letter of SingaporE
to shy is to throw or sling, as at a coconut shy

annotation.surface: Beer lovers sipping a cocktail and ducking any shots of spirits.
annotation.walkthrough: A Singapore sling is a gin cocktail, so ‘sling’ looks welded to Singapore; it is a separate verb meaning throw. ‘Shots’ in the definition are photographs, not drinks.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone camera-shy avoids having photographs, or shots, taken; the question mark flags the pun on drinks.

clue.text: Blunder due, without international language being recalled (3,4)

indicators.note: without means lacking here, so the letter is taken away
something recalled is called back, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: due is OWING; take away I for international
Lao is the language of Laos; reversed it reads OAL

annotation.surface: A slip in an exam, with an international language being called to mind.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Due’ is owing, as money is owed. An own goal in football is one a player accidentally scores against their own side.
annotation.definitionFit: An own goal is figuratively any blunder that harms your own cause.

clue.text: Force out European citizen without reserve (5)

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the reserve's letters come off the citizen

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation
a citizen is a SUBJECT; take away SUB, a reserve player

annotation.surface: A demand to deport a European national with no hesitation.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Without reserve’ reads as ‘unreservedly’, but the reserve is a substitute, SUB, removed from SUBJECT.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to throw someone out, as from a club or a pilot's seat.

clue.text: Section of Jenga almost lands together (4)

indicators.note: almost the whole word, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: a Jenga tower is built of wooden blocks; BLOCK loses its last letter

annotation.surface: A player's Jenga piece nearly lands, holding the tower together.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Lands’ looks like a verb for something falling, but it is the noun: countries.
annotation.definitionFit: A bloc is a group of countries allied together, as in the Eastern bloc.

clue.text: Grandiloquent writer to come back around, claiming genius but lacking English (10)

indicators.note: turned around, so the word runs backwards
to claim something is to take hold of it, so the reversed word surrounds the genius
lacking means without, so the E is removed

blocks.note: hair or plants that regrow come back; turned round it reads WORGER
a genius at something is a DEMON; take away E for English

annotation.surface: A pompous author making a comeback, claiming genius but having no grasp of English.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Come back’ looks like a return to form, but it is regrowing, turned round. A demon, as in a demon at chess, is someone brilliant at something.
annotation.definitionFit: A wordmonger is a writer who uses words showily or for effect, fairly called grandiloquent.

clue.text: One might like 16’s tail more elegant (3,7)

blocks.note: to tail someone is to follow them, to dog them
fancier means more elaborate or elegant

annotation.surface: A tale about which dog has the smarter tail.
annotation.walkthrough: 16 across is SALUKI, a hound, so the one who likes it is a dog lover. ‘16’s tail’ looks like the saluki's tail, but ’s is ‘is’ and ‘tail’ is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A dog fancier is an enthusiast for dogs, so might well like a saluki.

clue.text: Fashionable? That’s what was said about gold tooth (7)

indicators.note: about as in turned about, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: what's fashionable is in
sic is inserted in a quotation to mean ‘that is what was written’; turned about it reads CIS
or is gold in heraldry

annotation.surface: A question about fashion, and gossip about someone's gold tooth.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘About gold’ looks like a topic, but ‘about’ turns SIC round, and gold comes after it.
annotation.definitionFit: An incisor is one of the narrow cutting teeth at the front of the mouth.

clue.text: Court may require this number eight seed? (4)

blocks.note: an oat is a cereal grain, a seed
H is the eighth letter of the alphabet

annotation.surface: A tennis court needing its number eight seed.
annotation.walkthrough: The seeds of a tennis tournament are ranked, so ‘number eight seed’ sounds like a player; it is H after OAT. The seed comes first in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A witness in a law court is required to swear an oath before giving evidence.

clue.text: I don’t recall debut of Michael Caine as staggering (8)

definitions.note: the definition is what the answer would say; an amnesiac is a person who does not recall

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so take the first letter
letters that stagger lurch about, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: the first letter of Michael
anagram fodder

annotation.surface: An actor who can't remember seeing Michael Caine's astonishing first film.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Staggering’ reads as ‘amazing’, praise for Caine's debut, but it is the anagram instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: ‘I don’t recall’ is exactly what an amnesiac, someone who has lost their memory, would say.

clue.text: Where spoon goes for it? (2,3,4)

blocks.note: literally, the place a spoon is dipped at a meal
informal British for ‘in trouble’, as in ‘you’re for it now’

annotation.surface: A question about where you put your spoon.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one riddle about cutlery, but ‘for it’ is a separate idiom meaning in trouble, and the question mark flags the literal reading.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom both ways: to be in the soup and to be for it both mean facing trouble, and the soup is also literally where the spoon goes.

clue.text: Hound backers out of traditional part of Boxing Day party (6)

indicators.note: the backers of a word are its back letters, and each one is taken out

blocks.note: Boxing Day, 26 December, is when British shops hold their SALE; drop the E
UKIP, the UK Independence Party; drop the P

annotation.surface: Hounding the supporters out of a festive party.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Backers’ reads as political supporters of the party, but it means the back letters of both words. Boxing Day is the British holiday on 26 December.
annotation.definitionFit: A saluki is a tall, slender hunting hound from the Middle East.

clue.text: Like to look up Ken Loach movie souvenirs (9)

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: as means like
to peek is to look
Kes is Ken Loach's 1969 film about a boy and his kestrel

annotation.surface: A fan looking up Ken Loach films and collecting mementoes of them.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down clue ‘up’ reverses what comes before it, so both halves of the first part are turned round together, and only then is the film tacked on.
annotation.definitionFit: Keepsakes are small things kept in memory of someone or something, souvenirs.

clue.text: Slight help for diabetics dropping in time (6)

indicators.note: to drop something is to let it go, so IN leaves the word

blocks.note: INSULIN with IN removed
the standard abbreviation

annotation.surface: A small help for diabetics arriving just in time.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Dropping in’ looks like visiting, but it tells you to drop the letters IN.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the noun sense: a snub or affront.

clue.text: Someone who’s got fresh bread item from bakery under courier (7)

blocks.note: UPS is a parcel delivery company
a tart is a baked pastry; in a down clue it sits under UPS

annotation.surface: A baker's customer who has just picked up a loaf and a pastry from the courier.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Fresh bread’ belongs with the bakery picture, but ‘bread’ is slang for money: the upstart has new money. So the definition runs further than it seems.
annotation.definitionFit: An upstart has risen suddenly to wealth or position, someone with freshly acquired bread, or money.

indicators.note: in a down clue, what is under something sits below it, so TART follows UPS

clue.text: Who falls for fun truant keeping you distracted at first (8)

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so the truant holds the letters
take the first letter of each word

blocks.note: a skiver, in British slang, is someone who dodges school or work
the first letters of You Distracted

annotation.surface: A truant who has you so distracted you fall for his fun.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Falls for’ suggests being taken in, but it is literal: a skydiver falls out of a plane for pleasure.
annotation.definitionFit: A skydiver is someone who jumps from aircraft and free-falls for sport.

clue.text: Didn’t acknowledge or deign to move (7)

indicators.note: letters made to move change places

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: Someone who refused to acknowledge another or even deign to budge.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Deign’ sits so naturally beside ‘acknowledge’ that it passes as part of the picture rather than fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: To ignore someone is to fail to acknowledge them.

clue.text: Accessories for jumper’s neck when cycling (4)

indicators.note: cycled letters go round, so the last one comes to the front

blocks.note: to neck is British slang for to kiss; move the last S to the front

annotation.surface: Accessories to wear on a jumper's neck when out on a bike.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Jumper’ is British for a sweater, and a neck and accessories fit it perfectly; here it is a ski jumper, and ’s means ‘is’.
annotation.definitionFit: Skis are the equipment a ski jumper wears.

clue.text: Quite nice answer (5)

blocks.note: nice means kind
the standard abbreviation

annotation.surface: A lukewarm reply: the answer was quite nice.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Quite nice’ reads as one phrase, but ‘quite’ is the whole definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Kinda, informal for ‘kind of’, means quite or somewhat.

clue.text: A writ’s seen to alter who’s heard in court? (10)

indicators.note: to alter something is to change it, so the letters change order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: A lawyer's writ being redrafted to change which witness is heard in court.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Heard in court’ reads as ‘called to give evidence’, but it also describes someone who heard what happened. The question mark flags the double reading.
annotation.definitionFit: An earwitness testifies to what they heard, and is also someone heard in court.

clue.text: Is resident of 2 perhaps shown up without carbon fibre? (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read upwards, so the word runs backwards
without means lacking, so C is removed

blocks.note: used as is

blocks.clueFragment: resident of 2 perhaps shown up without carbon
blocks.note: a Manx person is a CELT, perhaps; reversed it reads TLEC, then lose C for carbon

annotation.surface: A question whether someone from the Isle of Man has been exposed as lacking carbon fibre.
annotation.walkthrough: 2 down is ISLE OF MAN, whose people count among the Celts; ‘perhaps’ marks that as an example.
annotation.definitionFit: Istle is a strong fibre from Mexican agave and yucca plants, used for cord and brushes.

clue.text: I oppose Erdogan tag on Istanbul cops (10)

definitions.note: the definition is what the answer would say; an antagonist is a person who opposes

indicators.note: to cop something is to catch hold of it, so the phrase holds the answer

blocks.note: erdogAN TAG ON ISTanbul

annotation.surface: A protester opposing an electronic tag that Istanbul police put on Erdogan.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Cops’ looks like the police of Istanbul, but it is the verb: the phrase cops, or catches, the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: ‘I oppose’ is the motto of an antagonist, one who actively opposes another.

clue.text: Current representative for Sprite (3)

blocks.note: I is the symbol for electric current
a Member of Parliament represents a constituency

annotation.surface: A current spokesman for a lemon-lime soft drink.
annotation.walkthrough: Sprite is a fizzy drink brand, which pulls ‘current representative’ towards advertising; the capital hides the small mischievous spirit.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a small mischievous spirit of folklore.

clue.text: Carefully examine Playboy? (4)

blocks.note: the verb sense: to search through thoroughly, as with a garden tool combing the ground
a dissolute man of fashion, as in Hogarth's Progress

annotation.surface: An instruction to scrutinise an issue of Playboy magazine.
annotation.walkthrough: Playboy with a capital looks like the magazine, but it is the dissolute man.
annotation.definitionFit: To rake is to search or scan carefully, and a rake is a pleasure-seeking libertine.

clue.text: Hollywood location scout finally getting report about portable tech (6)

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the scout's last letter is used
one thing about another goes round it

blocks.note: Hollywood is in Los Angeles
a report is a bang, a pop
the last letter of scouT

annotation.surface: A film location scout at last filing a report on a portable gadget.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Report’ looks like a written account, which suits a scout, but it is a loud noise.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a portable computer that rests on the lap.

clue.text: Pretentious to add Brussels sprouts? (8)

blocks.note: a postscript, PS, is something added to a letter
Brussels is the seat of the European Union
sprouts are a dish, by way of example

annotation.surface: A snob thinking it affected to add Brussels sprouts to the menu.
annotation.walkthrough: ‘Brussels sprouts’ is a single vegetable, but it splits: Brussels stands for the EU, and sprouts are an example of a dish.
annotation.definitionFit: Pseudish, from the British slang pseud, means pretentious or affected.
